justice: The narrow lane is dominated by parked cars and several parked scooters, leaving limited dedicated space for pedestrians and cyclists.
There is no clearly marked sidewalk or protected cycling space, so street space is not evenly allocated across different road users.
No curb ramps, tactile paving, or other visible barrier-free elements appear along the street edge, weakening accessibility for diverse users.
safety: The roadway is very narrow, and parked vehicles on both sides create conflict points and reduce maneuvering space for all users.
Dense low-hanging utility wires and a utility pole positioned within the street corridor contribute to a cluttered and potentially hazardous environment.
The absence of marked crossings, lane markings, and visible traffic-calming devices makes user priority and movement rules unclear.
livability: The street appears primarily residential, with apartment balconies, windows, and laundry indicating daily living activity.
However, there are no visible benches, public gathering spots, or active ground-floor amenities that would support social interaction in the street.
The confined alley-like form, parked vehicles, and limited greenery reduce the sense of openness and everyday street vitality.
sustainability: No street trees, planting strips, or visible green infrastructure are present, indicating weak ecological support and little heat or stormwater mitigation.
A bicycle is visible, suggesting some low-carbon travel is possible, but there is no dedicated bike lane or formal bike parking support.
The paving is almost entirely hard surface, and no permeable landscape features or rainwater management elements are visible.
aesthetics: The repetitive residential building facades create some visual consistency, but the overall scene feels monotonous and utilitarian.
Exposed overhead cables, wall-mounted air-conditioning units, and irregular attachments on facades create strong visual clutter.
The lack of trees, planting, and designed streetscape elements limits visual softness and reduces overall attractiveness.
comfort: There is almost no visible tree canopy or shade vegetation, so thermal comfort would be poor during hot weather despite some building shadow.
No benches, resting points, or pedestrian amenities are visible along the corridor, reducing physical comfort for people spending time outdoors.
The narrow enclosed street, visual clutter from cables, and close proximity of vehicles to walking space can reduce psychological comfort.
walkability: There is no continuous raised sidewalk; pedestrians appear to share the same narrow paved surface with cars and scooters.
Parked cars and scooters encroach on the already limited edge space, making walking routes less direct and less comfortable.
No visible crosswalks, curb extensions, or pedestrian-priority markings are present to support legible and safe walking movement.
bikeability: The street lacks any dedicated bike lane, painted markings, or physical protection for cyclists.
Parked cars and scooters narrow the usable travel path, increasing dooring and weaving risks for people cycling.
Although a bicycle is present, there is no visible formal bicycle parking or cycling-supportive infrastructure to make riding convenient.
